VISITORS IN GALLERY-HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS, GUESTS OF OTTAWA ROTARY CLUB
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to draw the attention of all hon. members to a representative group of young Canadians from collegiate institutes and high schools in many parts of Canada who are distinguished visitors in the galleries this afternoon. These students, numbering 132, are the guests of the Ottawa Rotary club, which, in association with well over one hundred other Rotary clubs in Canada, deserves high praise and credit for this outstanding adventure in citizenship promotion, furnishing, as it does, a very special opportunity for these fine samples of young Canada to gain a firsthand appreciation of the beauties and facilities of our national capital and the workings of our free democratic way of life at the national level.
As a Rotarian myself I take deep pride in calling their presence today to the attention of the House of Commons, at the same time extending to our visitors on behalf of all hon. members a warm and enthusiastic welcome to parliament hill.

Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): I wish to lay on the table a copy in English and in French of the general report of the plan for a national capital, and the letter of transmittal from the chairman of the federal district commission, together with the recommendations made to the federal district commission by the national capital planning committee.
These documents will be available for distribution to hon. members, and there will be an opportunity in the consideration of the estimates for an expression of appreciation to the members of the federal district commission, the national capital planning committee and the Gatineau park advisory board.
I believe hon. members would wish me to express at once our appreciation of the devotion to a national cause that has been exhibited over the years by the members of these commissions and boards, and by those who have supplied them with their technical advice and assistance in the preparation of this work. I am sure hon. members will find that this is a plan for a long-time job to be done by the Canadian people to testify to the continuity of their institutions and their pride in those institutions. Hon. members will feel, I am sure, that it is a privilege for us of this generation to have some part in the furtherance of that national scheme.
I am certain it will be a pleasure to the young ladies and young gentlemen who are guests of the house in the galleries today to have been present when the final plan for the national capital was placed before their elected representatives.

May I suggest, however, that these plans should not be regarded as providing only a beautiful community which will house the buildings in which the business of the nation is done, but also as being directed to the beautification of a city which

National Capital Plan to all Canadians is the capital of a nation which is assuming increasing importance in the world.
In every country, the capital city is something more than just a city. In a way it is an expression of the loyalties, the hopes and the expectations of the future. To the people of the United Kingdom, London is no mere city. It is the home of all that they cherish in the form of the great traditions of that nation with which we have been and will continue to be so closely associated. So it is with Paris, and with all the memories of the pride and glory of that other nation with which we have such deep and affectionate ties. So it is with Italy, where Rome holds the memories of their greatness in the past and their hopes for the future. So it is with every nation.
As we accept these plans, and as we have an opportunity to consider them, I hope there will be in the minds of all of us the belief that in the years ahead Ottawa is to be the capital of a nation of increasing importance which will give to all its people reason for pride in calling this their capital city.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question relates to the beauty of Ottawa and the parliament buildings. During the months I am in Ottawa I live up in room 669, which is a small office. I am not fussy, but there are no conveniences-not even running water. It is all right for me. I do have, however, a good many visitors, among whom are many students. There is a window in that office, and the first thing a student wants to do is to put his head out the window and take a look. What does he look at? He looks at the library of parliament, that tower, and what does he see? Some years ago the glass in those windows was broken, and they are now covered by boards. The glass has not yet been replaced. I wonder if the Minister of Public Works would consider replacing that glass to make the view more attractive.
The thing that really makes me grumble is the lack of a bridge across the Ottawa river. This bridge should have been built fifty years ago, and when the minister is considering my problem he could also keep that in mind.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this motion came before the house last night I indicated that the official opposition wished to take the opportunity which such a motion affords to bring before the house and the country the question of the opposition which exists to the suggestion that the British North America Act should be amended to allow the provinces to impose an indirect sales tax to the extent of three per cent.
Last night before the house adjourned I had dealt with some of the aspects of this matter, which might be briefly summarized as follows:	It is now established that the
proposal for an amendment in order to revise the old age pensions scheme and the amendment with regard to the three per cent sales tax are entirely separate; that this separation was brought about mainly as a result of the representations made by the provincial premiers, who had desired that the two matters should be considered separately, and their request was acceded to by the federal authorities, as outlined in a letter by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) on April 16.
There is, therefore, at this time no pressure with respect to the three per cent sales tax amendment, no pressure which could result in the fact that it might be said to be necessary in order to bring about an amendment to facilitate the revised scheme for old age pensions. Therefore this house can now express its opinion on the three per cent sales tax question entirely without pressure, and without any suggestion that to oppose the one amendment might jeopardize the introduction or the facilitation of an amendment dealing with the old age pensions scheme. So we have arrived at the point where we can consider the sales tax amendment entirely upon its merits.
Just before eleven o'clock last night I had suggested also some grounds for opposing the three per cent sales tax amendment. The first ground is that it is unnecessary that there should be any such amendment to the constitution. It is unnecessary that the provinces be empowered to impose indirect taxation, because they now have the power

to do the same thing, namely, to raise revenue by a turnover tax, provided that that levy is in the form of direct taxation.
There are several provinces which have such a form of taxation. Notably I have in mind the province of British Columbia, where it is at the rate of three per cent, and yields in a fiscal year, in round figures, the sum of $28 million from the taxpayers of that province.
The second objection to the proposed amendment is that it would enable the provinces to impose a hidden form of taxation. Much has been written in economic textbooks about the objection to hidden forms of taxes. I think, however, the matter has never been more succinctly or clearly expressed, and in language that those who are not economists can understand, than in a recent editorial in the Windsor Daily Star of April 5 of this year. It says:
The difference between the direct sales tax and the turnover tax is that the sales tax is added1 to the amount charged for an article and is known to the customer, but the turnover tax is on turnover and is hidden. The customer is charged so much and he does not know how much is tax. So far as that goes, he usually thinks the merchant is sticking him for a higher price and does not realize he is paying a tax.
Apart from this feature there is the unfair burden a turnover tax places on those least able to pay. It applies to everything. Those in poorer circumstances pay much more in proportion than those in higher incomes.
Then the article concludes:
The idea of a turnover tax is a cowardly method of raising revenues. It sticks the tax knife into the customer after he has been given an anaesthetic.
Perhaps the most important of the objections to this type of taxation is that it is directly inflationary. It is imposed at the manufacturer's level, based on turnover. Each succeeding dealer, whether he be the middleman distributor, or retailer, adds to the price of the goods, which already includes a tax, his normal margin of profit. Through each succeeding pair of hands that particular article passes there is an increased mark-up, based on the initial price plus the tax, with the result that the tax at three per cent at origin may well be an additional increase in price of from five to six per cent by the time it reaches the hands of the consumer.
This type of taxation increases the prices of goods people must buy, out of all proportion to the revenue it actually brings to the treasury. It increases profits, because the mark-up is placed on the tax as well as on the initial price of the goods. To that extent it directly increases prices, increases profits and contributes directly to inflation. It is inequitable in that it bears most heavily on those who are least able to pay, because the
Turnover Tax
man with a low income and a large family has to pay as much tax on the goods he buys as the man who has a large income and perhaps only a small family.
These are the objections on economic grounds which might be advanced with respect to the tax. There are other objections, not the least of which is that at the present time we have much too large a proportion of our taxation being raised by way of indirect taxes. In years gone by-and not so many years at that-the major proportion of the revenue of the federal government and of most provincial governments came from direct taxation. That trend has now been reversed to a point where practically fifty per cent-I believe in 1949 it was over fifty per cent-of the national revenue is raised by means of indirect taxation.
Looking at the figures tabled by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, we find that the federal government now raises $1,200 million by means of indirect taxation. This amounts to forty per cent of the revenue collected by the federal government. If one bears in mind that the federal sales tax has just been increased to the general level of ten per cent, and the fact that the proposed amendment would enable the provinces to impose a similar tax of three per cent, both taxes being applied at the source on turnover, one will see, as was shown by an analysis made by experts on the subject, that the increases in prices of the goods when they reach the hands of the consumers would be in the order of from sixteen to eighteen per cent. With the burden of inflation and heavy taxation now being borne by the Canadian people reflected directly in higher prices and a spiralling cost of living, it surely cannot be denied that a tax impost which would result, when coupled with the federal government tax, in an increase in price of from sixteen to eighteen per cent should not be contemplated at the moment.
Another objection which might be offered is that the power to the provinces to impose this tax would be divisive and discriminatory. All the provinces do not now have equal sources of revenue. Some provinces have indicated that they would not resort to the three per cent tax. Other provinces have indicated that they would definitely impose the three per cent tax, and in fact would like to impose it at a higher rate.
If one of the objects of- recent dominion-provincial financial discussions, from 1945 forward, has been, as I understand it, to distribute equitably among the people of the country the fiscal burden they

have to bear, so that the poorer provinces particularly would be in receipt o f provincial incomes which would enable them to render services comparable with the services rendered by the richer provinces, with respect to social security; and if generally the idea has been that there should be a redistribution of income among the provinces, perhaps on the basis of fiscal need-if, as I say, that is an accurate statement of the general approach to the problem, then I submit that this proposal to allow the provinces to levy a three per cent sales tax would be a complete negation of that principle.
This is true for the very .reasons I have pointed out; some provinces which are in a fortunate position say they would not use the tax, even if the power to use it were granted, and other provinces say that as soon as the power is granted they intend to use it, and indeed would like to have authority to impose a tax of perhaps four per cent or even more.
Other provinces say they would like to apply the tax not only on the sale of goods but also on the rendering of services such as electric power, theatres, hotels and all that sort of thing. It would render quite unequal the cost of living as between the various provinces. A person passing from coast to coast and stopping off in the various provinces would find an entirely different cost of living in each province. It is a form of taxation which is unnecessary and particularly vicious, in that it would be discriminatory as between the provinces and the people living in the provinces. The very fact that the suggestion should now be put forward indicates that dominion-provincial financial relations are in pretty much of a mess as a result of the policies pursued by this government over past years, particularly as a result of their failure to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference which sat first in 1945 and completely overhaul the fiscal system of this country and follow it through to a logical and successful conclusion.
The provinces were practically driven by the federal authority into such a position that they very reluctantly, in many cases, gave up certain taxation powers. As a result of this whole process the provinces are now offered a most unpopular, a most unsatisfactory and most uneconomical form of taxation, namely, a sales tax. That is the position at which we have arrived. The provinces are strapped for funds as the result of the dominion-provincial agreements which have been imposed on them by the federal government, and are now in such a position that they have to contemplate asking for power

to impose an unjust, unfair and discriminatory sales tax on their people in order to get revenue.
The final consideration I should like to lay before the house in asking it to pass its opinion on the amendment which I shall move is that there is a very strong body of opinion which holds that this is an entirely wrong method to use to bring about a change of the constitution in this respect. We have been witnessing a development under which eleven officials, ten from the provincial governments and one from the federal government, are undertaking to amend our constitution in fundamental particulars, with regard to the division of taxing powers between the central and provincial governments.
The division of taxing powers was laid down first in the British North America Act by the fathers of confederation. After years of study and conference they arrived at the division that we now have. Although it may well be suggested that the time has come when a revision of that distribution is necessary, I think the strongest objection should be raised to an alteration in our constitution in any fundamental respect being brought about by eleven people, none of them elected for that purpose. I am not being personally critical of any of the people who have taken part in the conference, but I think that if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who has carried forward most of the negotiations with the provincial premiers, will analyse the situation he will agree that he was not elected, nor was any provincial premier elected, to amend the constitution. That is not one of the things which the people of the provinces or of the dominion had in mind when they voted in either provincial or dominion elections. But eleven men are seeking to take to themselves the power to amend the constitution in perhaps its most important particular, the distribution of financial powers as between the federal and provincial governments.
In support of my contention that this is a wrong method to use to amend the constitution, I should like to quote from an editorial by Mr. Sandwell in the last issue of the Toronto Saturday Night. He points out that none of these eleven people was elected to assume the responsibility they are now assuming, and in the course of his editorial he says:
The correct position, it seems to this column, is that neither the government of the dominion nor the governments of the ten provinces have any right to change the distribution of taxing powers, or any other arrangement of the powers of legislation and administration, that are established by the British North America Act. The dominion parliament- wrongly, we believe-has acquired from the British

parliament the right to change the constitution in respect of the classes of subjects assigned to that parliament's legislative power. It has not, so far as we can see, acquired any right to change, with or without the consent of one, two, six or ten of the provinces, the extent of those classes, and yet that is exactly what it is purporting to do.
The whole idea of the amendment of the constitution becoming a matter of bargaining between the dominion government of the moment and the ten provincial governments of the moment seems to us illogical, undemocratic and revolting.
In conclusion I desire to move, seconded by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that further consideration should not be given to the proposal to authorize by amendment to the British North America Act an indirect provincial sales tax of three per cent."
On a recent occasion when we were discussing the proposal to increase the federal sales tax from eight to ten per cent, all members, on the opposition side at any rate, were agreed that that proposal was unnecessary at the present time and that this form of taxation is generally undesirable, because it is hidden, because it is inflationary, and because it would increase the already heavy burden of the high cost of living. All members of the Social Credit party, the C.C.F. party and the official opposition were united in opposing that increase. I am confident that those members will be united again on this occasion.
Since this is a proposal which invites an expression of opinion from the house and does not in any way involve legislation presented by the government, I would hope that members on the government side might feel free to express their opinion, because that is all they are being asked to do by the amendment-to consider or reject the proposal that at this time there should be no power given to the provinces to increase the cost of living by the imposition of a three per cent indirect sales tax.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will consider whether or not this amendment is in order, and I do not intend to discuss the question. I do wish to point out some of the inaccuracies1-quite involuntary, I am sure- in the speech of the hon. member who has moved this motion. His very first words last evening in opening this matter, which I find at page 3257 of Hansard, were:
Before this motion carries, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the house. It concerns the proposal which has been made by the federal government to the various provincial governments to amend the British North America Act so as to enable the provinces to impose an indirect sales tax or turnover tax of three per cent.
Turnover Tax
I am sure the hon. member must know that is not a proposal that was made to the provinces by the federal government. A conference was called of the provincial governments, which met here in December of last year. At the end of that conference an agreed statement was issued to the press, which is to be found at page 137 of the report of the proceedings of the conference of federal and provincial governments, Ottawa, December 4-7, 1950, headed "Statement to the press by the Right Honourable Louis S. St. Laurent at the conclusion of the conference." I quote:
The conference discussed:
1.	The offer of the federal government for new tax agreements.
2.	The offer of the federal government respecting old age security.
3.	A provincial proposal for an amendment to the constitution to permit the provincial legislatures to levy an indirect sales tax at the retail level.
Why should the hon. member wish to create the impression that this proposal was made by the federal government, when it is perfectly clear, from the statement agreed to and issued after the conference, that it was a provincial proposal that was made at that time?

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: What province made that proposal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
Several provinces made the proposal, and it was generally discussed. I think the first to voice it at that conference was the premier of New Brunswick. I believe the hon. member will find that at page 30 of the report of these proceedings. I do not think it was referred to by any of those who spoke before the premier of New Brunswick, whose speech commences at page 29 of the report. This is the way he put it:
This, however, prompts me to suggest that there is another constitutional amendment which should be considered at the same time. It has relation to the taxing powers of the provinces whose jurisdiction under the British North America Act is limited to direct taxation.
Under the authority so vested in them, five of the provinces have now in operation a consumer's tax, so-called. In effect it is a sales tax but cannot be imposed in that less unattractive form. In 1950 the legislature of New Brunswick adopted legislation authorizing such a tax, notwithstanding the problems presented in its collection. It is quite possible that as time passes other provinces will find it necessary to rely upon this method of taxation to meet their revenue requirements.
We hope that all provinces will agree that a constitutional amendment should be sought to permit such a levy through the simple expedient of a sales tax. One would assume that if the provinces are in agreement on this point the federal authorities would readily concur.
That is the manner in which this arose. At that time the federal government had proposed to the provinces new tax agreements, had called the attention of the premiers to

Turnover Tax
the report of the joint committee of the two houses of parliament on old age security, and had stated that if it found a constitutional amendment necessary to enable contributions to be attached to a no-means-test old age pension it would attempt to implement at the earliest possible moment the recommendations of that joint committee. I think it was considered by the public generally that it would be desirable to have that kind of amendment made to the constitution.
At the same time, and concurrently with this general conference, there was an adjourned conference of the provincial premiers to discuss the method by ' which amendtnents to the constitution should be made in Canada. We had been discussing these matters on their merits in an amicable and cordial manner, and it appeared that it would not have been conducive to maintaining that cordial and amicable manner of discussing the problem if we said: No; so far as we are concerned all' amendments must be just one way amendments; there must be no amendment transferring any part of the federal powers to provincial legislatures; they must be amendments transferring some part of provincial jurisdiction to the federal parliament. We did not think an attitude of that kind would have been, conducive to the discussion of these matters in the spirit which was being displayed by all those who were then in conference.
The hon. member chooses to say that this constitutes an offer by the federal government to the provinces to take jurisdiction to impose an indirect sales tax. Well, he may view that as he likes, but he cannot change the facts, nor can he change the printed report or the agreed statement.
The hon. member goes on to say that we have now reached the point where it is admitted that the 'wo constitutional amendments are entirely separate and can be treated in that way, and that this is due to the insistence of the premier of Nova Scotia in a letter of April 16.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: That is not quite accurate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
The hon. member should have read the correspondence more carefully if he was going to make an assertion such as that. Had he read it more carefully he would have seen that in a letter dated March 12 the premier of New Brunswick had this to say, the letter appearing at page 2729 of Hansard:
Some confusion seems to have developed' in certain quarters-
That was even before it developed in Kamloops.
-where an opinion or view has developed that the sales tax amendment was part and parcel of the

old' age pension plan which was under study at the December federal-provincial conference. All governments there represented are fully aware that there is no relation or connection between the two and that the old age pension plan can go forward without any sales tax amendment.
Then he added:
In order, however, to emphasize this point I am referring herein only to the old age pension amendment and shall make the proposals regarding a sales tax amendment the subject of another letter to follow shortly.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) replied to that letter fully, agreeing that there was no connection whatever between the two amendments. The one concerning old age pensions can go forward without any sales tax amendment.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
When was that first put into
writing by the federal authorities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
That was first put forward by the federal authorities at the very opening of the conference. It was stated that the tax agreements, old age pensions and the matter of the sales tax could all be considered separately. The tax agreements were not dependent upon agreement on old age pensions, and old age pensions were not dependent upon agreement on the tax agreements. Those were the two proposals put before the conference by the federal government, and the only proposals put before the conference by the federal government. It was only upon this question being raised afterwards by Premier McNair that we did not take the stand that we would not give consideration to their request, if they all wanted that power, to impose an indirect sales tax.
After all, in spite of what may be said by any editor of any newspaper in Canada, the provincial premiers do have a certain representative capacity when they meet with the federal government. They are elected to look after the interests of the people of their provinces, just as we are elected to look after the interests of Canadians generally without regard to the province in which they happen to have their homes. I believe that if ten provincial premiers, having given serious study and consideration to a problem, come together and say that in their opinion and judgment it would be in the interests of the people of their provinces to have a certain form of taxation available to them, it would be, I shall say, impertinent for the federal government-in whatever aspect it may be regarded when it comes from the hon. member for Kamloops-to say the proposal is so ridiculous that we will not give it any consideration whatever. Certainly that would not be an attitude that would be conducive to obtaining the kind of co-operation between those who exercise legislative and

administrative authority in this country that is desirable for the promotion of the interests of the people.
I am not going to discuss the merits or demerits of an indirect sales tax. The hon. member for Kamloops says it would bring about discrimination. He himself stated that there was that kind of discrimination. He says that in his province there is now a direct sales tax of three per cent that is payable by all those who are either residing in his province or who just happen to be there and want to buy some commodities. There are at least five provinces in which there are no such sales taxes. There is one in which the sales tax, instead of being three per cent, is five per cent. This kind of discrimination has existed, and the people of Canada have carried on. Since those discriminatory measures were put into effect there have been provincial elections, and those who were responsible for putting them into effect got the support of the majority of the elected members in their respective provinces. That seems to be the way in which democratic institutions operate in this country.
The hon. member says that this kind of tax would be a tax put on at the manufacturers' level, and would pyramid in the hands of each successor who dealt with the same commodity. There again I am afraid the hon. member has been rather shortsighted in reading the form of the amendment which the Minister of Justice was asked by the ten premiers to approve, which he did approve, and which he sent out to them with his letter of January 2, 1951. It is printed on page 43 of Hansard of February 1, and reads as follows:
(b) indirect taxation within the province in respect of the sale of goods (except goods sold for shipment outside the province) to a buyer for purposes of consumption or use and not for resale . . .
It is apparent that the hon. member has built up a windmill against which to direct his speech and his motion, without regard to the documentary evidence that he had before him.
The hon. member says that amendments to the constitution should not be made by eleven men. If that means anything, I believe it does convey the implication that there are amendments made in that way, or that are being proposed to be made in that way. The hon. member knows that there have been a certain number of amendments to the constitution of this country since 1867, and that for the last fifty years at least the procedure which has become the established procedure is for those amendments to be made by the parliament at Westminster on a joint address of the two houses of the Canadian parliament. No one who has been 80709-209
Turnover Tax
prime minister of Canada has at any time attempted to make amendments to the constitution. The government from time to time has recommended to the houses of parliament that a joint address be presented to His Majesty requesting that an amendment be made. The joint address does not go forward until the members of this house, and the members of the other place, have had an opportunity of deciding, by a majority of the votes of the elected or appointed representatives of the people, whether it is in their interest that the amendment should be made.
The hon. member has been here long enough to have heard from that side of the house the thundering tones upbraiding the government for daring to suggest any kind of amendment to the constitution without the consent of the provincial governments. Frequently that has been the subject of strong denunciations from the other side of the house. The hon. member professes a devotion to democratic processes; then he suggests it is this house which should determine through what form the provincial authorities will put their consent when it is to be expressed to the presentation of an address for an amendment. This party feels that that is a responsibility for those who speak for the provincial government. I know that in fact several of them had their legislatures pass laws or resolutions in connection with the amendment which is now being sought from the parliament at Westminster to establish a no-means-test old age pension in this country. As to what the other governments did I do not know, and I do not think it should be my concern. If one should undertake to put its view forward as being the view of the whole province, the electors of that province will have a democratic opportunity to deal with its conduct. All the provincial legislatures having been in session since this dominion-provincial conference of last December, I am convinced that there was ample opportunity for those legislatures to make their views known and that the ten provincial premiers who have expressed their acceptance of the form of amendment to be requested with respect to old age pensions had the authority of the people of their respective provinces to express such consent. I am not going to deal with the merits of that situation. But this conference was adjourned.
From what I have read in the newspapers it seems that there are some of the provincial premiers who do not think that it would be a good thing for the provincial legislatures to have the right to resort to an

Turnover Tax
indirect sales tax at the retailers' level. Quite frankly, I would be sorry if they all agreed that there should be any transfer of taxing jurisdiction from parliament to the provincial legislatures. But at this time, when we are merely at the stage of an adjourned conference, both on the method of making future amendments to the constitution here in Canada by some Canadian authority, and on the question of further tax agreements between the federal government and the provinces, it would not appear as if this house had any confidence in this government if it were to say that it should withdraw from the subjects under discussion for the continuation of this conference the possibility of consideration being given to an amendment that would work to transfer some jurisdiction from the federal authority to the provincial authority.

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister permit a question at this point?

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: What attitude did he, on behalf of his government, take as to the propriety of the provinces having power to impose a three per cent sales tax by the necessary amendment?

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: I was not in a position where I could express the decision of the Canadian government. That was not a part of the authority that had been given to those who were representing the federal government in those conferences. If there was a unanimous request from the provincial governments for that kind of amendment at this period of our constitutional development, with the matters that are now pending for decision between the provincial authorities and the dominion government, I would recommend to my colleagues that we do not refuse to go along with them.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Even though it is a thoroughly bad tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Even though the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) calls it a thoroughly bad tax, and had the opportunity of having a vote in this house which showed in what a small minority he was.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Better hold your temper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: The fact that the hon. member calls the thing "thoroughly bad" does not necessarily mean that everyone in Canada agrees with him; because he has called this government thoroughly bad on more than one occasion and he has had ample evidence that there are not many in the country who agree with him.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Over fifty per cent of the people agree with him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: This strategy has another effect. This is a motion to say that this house is not prepared to go into committee of supply to provide this government with the money required to carry out the administration of the country. The amendment is that all the words after "that" be struck out and be replaced by this expression of no confidence in this government to carry on further discussions with the provincial authorities on a matter such as that which is involved in the terms of the amendment.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT

That is a far-fetched
assumption.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: The motion is that the house resolve itself into committee of supply to consider the estimates that have been placed before the house. This amendment seeks to express in advance an opinion upon something that may never come before the house. There could not be any attempt to amend the constitution in order to give the provinces the right to impose indirect sales tax without an address voted on affirmatively by this house. This amendment seeks to express the opinion that further consideration should not be given to the proposal to authorize, by amendment to the British North America Act, an indirect provincial sales tax of three per cent. There is no such proposal being given consideration by this house. A proposal was put forward by the provincial premiers at a conference which is now adjourned, and with respect to which their views were expressed-as to nine of them, I think-in the correspondence that has been tabled. I have read in the newspapers, since the dates of that correspondence, that some views were expressed by another provincial premier in a public speech at London recently.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Who was that? Was it the premier of Ontario?

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
I understand that the premier of Ontario, in a speech at London recently, expressed the opinion that it would not be desirable to have that kind of amendment. There is no direct expression of his views in the correspondence that has been tabled; but my understanding is that both he and the premier of Quebec have now expressed the opinion that it would not be desirable to have that kind of amendment. The premier of Quebec seems to be quite satisfied with the system that he has established of having the dealers act as collectors of a direct tax on the commodities that are sold to the consumers. As a matter of fact, the tax is five per cent in some cities. I

would not be at all surprised if it was preferred to raise five per cent in that manner rather than to be limited to raising three per cent in another manner.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: He would not be denied both ways, then, if an amendment passed, would he?

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: He would not be denied both ways; but it is something for which those administering public affairs would be responsible to the people of their respective provinces; and the hon. gentleman knows, as I do, that in provincial politics the volume of taxes and the form of taxes imposed by a party in power are always live issues at election time.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: That is in the provincial arena.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
That has been my experience over the last fifty years. Though I was not of his party, I was somewhat incensed over the fact that my good professor of Roman law was generally called "the taxer", he having headed a provincial administration during whose tenure of office some unpopular forms of taxation had been enacted. There is no doubt that all these taxes are rather obnoxious. But there is no doubt that present conditions in this country require methods whereby there are transfer payments from some income groups to other income groups. That has become necessary. We have discussed in this house problems with respect to social welfare, problems with respect to education, and the needs that are so urgent in all these public services. I think that these matters should be discussed on their merits, and that this house should wait until something comes before it, before it expresses any veto on proposals that may never come before it.
When we sit around the conference table with the elected representatives of the ten Canadian provinces, we are all fellow citizens 'interested in the same degree in the good administration of the affairs of the whole country under a system whereby a part of the sovereignty is in one place and another part of the sovereignty is in another place, and where the whole of the sovereignty has to be used to satisfy the legitimate interests of the people of the country. Well, when we do that I think that it is preferable that we try to arrive at the best possible solutions, and that we do not go there with a declaration made in advance that we will not even give consideration to any one thing that might come from the provincial representatives.

Turnover Tax
I think that we have to be prepared to give these matters consideration. It may very well be that the consensus will be that there should not be at this time any attempt to interfere with the respective taxation jurisdictions of these authorities. It may very well be the basis upon which we were acting at that time; that nothing was going to be decided by the majority; that unless there was unanimity with respect to any of those constitutional proposals they could not be proceeded with. That is the basis upon which the matter was put before the ten provincial governments. It was a transfer of jurisdiction, something which interested both the federal government and the provincial governments, and that in those cases until there was agreement that the provinces would be bound by a majority we would not attempt to proceed without the unanimous consent of all those who were to be affected.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: Does there look to be any possibility that the provinces will agree to any such change by a majority vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
Well, here I would not like to express any opinion. I know that there was no agreement to be bound by anything but unanimous consent so far; but they have not, any of them, declared that there was no use pursuing the matter further. They are still studying it, and still considering it, and I think they are considering it in good faith, and in an honest endeavour to serve the best interests of those whom they represent in their elected capacities. They have not said that there was no use pursuing it further.
This being a request by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) for a vote of no confidence in this government, of course the government cannot accept it. The government has confidence in itself. It hopes that there are enough members in the house to support it in that stand; but the rejection of this amendment does not mean anything at all. It does not mean that this house would be prepared to join in an address requesting an amendment to authorize a sales tax. It merely means that this house is not prepared to turn this government out because this government did not refuse to give consideration to that matter when it was raised in the dominion-provincial conference by one of the provincial premiers. That is all it means.
If ever there was any unanimous agreement by the provinces that they should have that power, the government would then have to take the responsibility of deciding whether or not it would recommend to parliament the adoption of an address; and if it recommended to parliament the adoption of an

Turnover Tax
address, parliament would then dispose of that address as the hon. members might feel was in the best interests of the Canadian people as a whole. But at this time there is certainly no such urgency of expressing such an opinion as would displace the urgency of getting on with the normal business of voting the supplies that are required for the administration of this country's affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has placed this motion upon the basis of a want of confidence motion, and has left the impression that to support it would be to vote want of confidence in the government. It seems to me that the words of this motion are not susceptible of such interpretation.
The words of this motion constitute an expression of opinion by hon. members that further consideration should not be given to the proposal to authorize, by amendment to the British North America Act, an indirect provincial sales tax of three per cent. That I submit is an appropriate motion at such a time. In fact, this is a long established practice. This is a procedure with a long tradition behind it.
The motion to go into supply affords an opportunity to obtain an expression by the house in regard to any matter that the house is competent to deal with. Obviously, a motion cannot deal with some other motion that is before the house. It cannot deal with any legislation that is before the house. It can deal only with something that is of concern to hon. members which is not before the house in any other way. That is exactly what we have in this instance.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this motion is not only a motion well within the rules, but it is a very proper thing that hon. members at this time should indicate what their opinion is in regard to this form of taxation, so that the time of this government, and of other governments, will not be wasted if in fact hon. members do not believe that any tax of this kind should be introduced. That is the purpose of the motion, and that is the result that would follow. The government then would have an indication of the sentiment of this house, and could very properly say that it did not consider it was wise to proceed with the discussion of an amendment of this kind to the British North America Act.
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, to a great deal of surprise as to why the Prime Minister should be so exercised about the fact that it was stated a proposal had been made. A great deal has been said -about where this suggestion came from. It was stated that the

suggestion had come from the premier of New Brunswick. That will undoubtedly be interesting to the people of New Brunswick. It is of course a matter of interest that New Brunswick already has a four per cent tax; and also it is a matter of interest that the premier of New Brunswick has indicated that he does not think that the amendment put forward by the dominion government-and it is an amendment put forward by the dominion government-is in itself adequate; because he wants an amendment which would make it possible to impose a four per cent indirect tax, or such higher tax as he sees fit.
In other words he has made it clear that he does not think there should be any limitation of this kind. Of course it would have the advantage of being a hidden tax. The premier of New Brunswick is within his rights in presenting that opinion, and the members of the House of Commons, who also must assume responsibility, are within their rights if they also express an opinion as to a tax of this kind.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are other reasons why I find it difficult to understand why such vigorous exception should have been taken to the word "proposal". In the house this subject has been under consideration before. It is interesting to note that this was brought forward for at least consideration by the house in the speech from the throne. If it was worthy of inclusion in the speech from the throne as something for members to consider, and if it was put forward by the governor general as such, then surely it is appropriate for us to discuss a resolution of this kind in an orderly way.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext: The Prime Minister just changed his mind, that is all.

subsubtopic: TURNOVER TAX OF THREE PER CENT
speechtext:
I would remind hon. members of the words in the speech from the throne when reference was made to these two proposed amendments to the British North America Act-and there were only two.' One was an amendment that would make it possible to proceed with the old age pensions plan, and the other was an amendment which would make it possible to introduce this new form of indirect taxation. There were just those two.
Therefore with that in mind it is interesting to read the words in the speech from the throne, and I quote from that document as it is recorded at page 2 of Hansard in the present session:

Because it is a live issue I suggest that it is appropriate that the members of this house express their opinions without any suggestion that such an expression of opinion would or would not be a vote of confidence in the government. In fact the Prime Minister has indicated that the government has not expressed an opinion. Since it has not expressed an opinion I suggest that it is preposterous to place on the basis of a vote of confidence an expression of opinion which would merely assist the Prime Minister in understanding what the sentiment of this house really is in regard to this tax.
Having dealt with that, let me refer to what the Prime Minister said about the British Columbia tax. He showed a measure of irritation that was out of keeping with the manner in which the arguments have been put forward. He was extremely sarcastic about what the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) had done in presenting some of his arguments and his references to the British Columbia tax.
The British Columbia tax is a sales tax. The Prime Minister left the inference that since they have already dealt with a tax of this kind there would not be much difference if they had this amendment. But the fact is that the British Columbia tax is a direct and open tax. I am not expressing any opinion in favour of a tax of that kind; in fact I have expressed an opinion to the contrary on other occasions, and I refer to when I had a certain responsibility in regard to provincial taxes of that nature. There is a vast difference between these two taxes. The direct provincial tax indicates clearly to the purchaser what the purchaser is paying, but this indirect tax is a hidden tax which hides from the purchaser what he is paying and is not in any way made up in the real value of the article itself.
They are very different and they create great differences in any goods that are merchandised on a national scale. Where goods are merchandised on a national scale the price can be fixed in the advertisements and the purchaser knows that that is the price. When a direct tax is paid the purchaser knows he is paying a tax. That is his choice; that is his decision. In this case, however,

the provinces would have the right to impose or not to impose a hidden tax. Consequently it would be made extremely difficult to merchandise on a national scale products of the same kind that are distributed throughout the whole of this country.
Let us look again at what the Prime Minister said. He said: I do not think it should be my concern. I think it should be his concern; I think it should be the concern of every member of this house whether this is the kind of amendment that should be brought forward. Following the Prime Minister this afternoon one was led to the conclusion that the Prime Minister had the idea that this was something for debate only in the provincial legislatures. If there was agreement, that settled it and we had nothing to do. This matter has been up before the House of Commons in years gone by and never before was there any suggestion that this was not a subject for discussion in the House of Commons. The fact is that the primary responsibility is in this house because it is from this house that any proposal must go forward for consideration by Westminster.
Having said that, and hoping that there still may be an expression by members of this house at this time, may I once again point out the reasons why there should be a clear declaration that this amendment will not be adopted by this house to meet any of the problems that we face today. First of all, let us remember that an amendment of this kind would change the fundamental allocation of taxation which has existed ever since 1867. There are many people who will say, "Well, we have come a long way from 1867." That is quite true, but those who drafted the basic constitution at that time could never have contemplated the problems we face today, and I am one of those here who for years have been urging that these changes should be recognized and that there should be a re-examination of the whole tax structure. I have urged over and over that there should be a conference which would deal exclusively with the whole problem of taxation, so there might be an allocation of taxes at the dominion, provincial and municipal levels which would bear most easily upon the taxpayers of this country and make it possible for the administrative responsibility of those bodies to be matched by their taxing authority so they could in fact have independent discretion as to what they should do.
The suggestion here would simply provide a temporary solution. It would break away from our traditional tax position without providing any satisfactory solution from the
Turnover Tax
long-term point of view. Why should the dominion government make an amendment to the basic constitution and say to the provinces, "You can just have a little 3 per cent nibble at this tax, and no more." Either it is right to let the provinces into the indirect field without any limiting declaration of that kind and have both fields open to provincial and federal governments, as they are now, or there should be clearly defined taxes available to both bodies. The dominion government should not say that the provinces should have so much of this and so much of that, and beyond that they can just whistle for it; that they can only do what may be possible within the amount the federal government is allowing them. That is not the basis on which it should be done.
I know that in answer to what I have just said it can be suggested that this cannot be done at all unless the provinces agree. That is so; but the provinces are being asked to consider-and I repeat "asked to consider"- a draft put forward by the dominion government which would impose that limitation at this time. Already we have an indication that one of the provinces does not think that is enough. Therefore we know that if this were done now it would not be very long before there would be a request for an increased amount. After all this is administrative in function, and should not be the subject of a constitutional amendment of this kind.
This form of indirect taxation not only carries with it all the objections which apply to any other indirect tax; it has special objections in addition. An indirect tax imposed by the dominion government would apply over the whole field evenly. An indirect tax which could be levied by some provincial governments and not by others would constitute in effect something in the nature of a tariff barrier between the provinces; and the amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice would not prevent evils of that kind creeping in. When he suggested the addition of the words "not so as to discriminate between sellers or classes of sellers of the same class of goods" he did not suggest anything that would prevent the inequities which would follow the application of a tax of this kind. Let us take just one of the absurdities that would be met. In the proposed amendment the Minister of Justice has placed before the provincial governments, there is a provision that this would not apply to goods shipped out of the province. Just think of the very interesting situation that would arise right here in Ottawa and in Hull, across the river. Anyone living in Ottawa could order goods

Then may I point out that this is a tax at the top level, at the retail level, and because of that fact it is a tax on every other tax that goes into the cost of goods in this country. Mr. Speaker, I rise not to discuss the merits or demerits of the proposed tax; I rise at this time because I think that the people of Canada must be badly confused about this question of old age pensions. For the last couple of years particularly most of the members of this house have been discussing the possibility of relieving the aged people of this country, and the government brought forward a program. That program was to abolish the means test at age 70 and to reduce the age limit to 65. That program has been pounded fairly thoroughly into the minds of the Canadian people.
Most of those who are affected think, as they have thought for some months, that at last the members of the House of Commons have got down to business and have worked out a formula whereby their problem is going to be taken care of. They are badly mixed up on that particular angle.
The second thing that they are badly mixed up on is this. We in this house discussed at great length the possibility of Canada's amending her own constitution. A great many nice speeches were made. We were told that Canada at last has grown up, that we go it alone, that from now on we decide our own destiny. Everybody assumed that we had that right, and that matters that were federal in scope could be decided in the House of Commons. But when we get the first test, what happens? The people outside write to members and say that the matter of old age pensions is a federal one. It is a matter dealt with by a federal act that was passed in the first place over the opposition of most of the provinces. After this country has grown up and we have taken the right to amend our own constitution, in order to abolish the means test with regard to old age pensions, we have to apply to the British parliament. The average person is asking himself:	In what respect has Canada taken
the right to decide her own destiny? Dominion-provincial conferences are called, and the premiers are brought in to decide what is to be done about these two important questions. In my opinion the decision was arrived at in 1945, and the program then brought in by the federal government is the program that we should be discussing in this house at this time. Instead of that we have the minutes of the last conference, and agreement was arrived at so far as the elimination of the means test is concerned. But the
Turnover Tax
other matter is just as important as the first one-the matter of lowering the age limit in the group 65 to 69. The real suffering in this country is in that age group. What is the solution? The solution was offered by the provinces. They said:	It is going to
cost us considerably more money to accept the lowered age limit. It is going to mean a lot more people on pension in the provinces, and we are going to pay 50 per cent of it.
The premier of Saskatchewan said that it would cost his province at least fourteen per cent more. That money has to be raised. The premier of Nova Scotia apparently considered the imposition of this sales tax very necessary, because in his last budget he budgeted for approximately $1 million which would be raised through this tax, and I think he was budgeting for a deficit of $2 million or $3 million. I would judge from that action that he considers this tax is necessary if he is to implement the lowering of the age limit.
In presenting his case to the dominion-provincial conference, the premier of Newfoundland stated that out of a population of
350,000	they had at that time about 11,000 on pension. He said that if the age limit were lowered it would mean not 11,000 on pension but 22,000. The number will be doubled, and it is an unbearable load to carry So far as Newfoundland is concerned.
To say that the question now before the house, the abolition of this idea of a hidden tax, has no connection with the second part of the program of old age pensions is not correct, because, in my opinion, they are tied together. Most of the provinces in this country will have to depend on raising new revenue somewhere, and this is the way it was suggested the revenue should be raised. In my opinion, you cannot divorce the two questions. It is definitely tied up with the full implementation of the old age pension program, and we are going to have to make decisions on it. Personally I am opposed to the hidden sales tax. We have been over the years, and I have not changed my opinion on it. But the thing I want to focus attention on is this. Let us not kid ourselves into thinking that, by moving a motion in the house that we are not going to pass the sales tax, we are not injuring the latter part of the program of lowering the age limit.
British Columbia might be able to handle her own problems, and possibly Alberta will. Saskatchewan says that they will have to raise fourteen per cent more money for that purpose. That is a problem. Perhaps Ontario can stand on its own feet, and also Quebec; but very definitely New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland are going to have

Turnover Tax
to get a revision in the existing agreements by way of subsidy, or new revenue will have to be found in the province if the sales tax is not to be proceeded with.
The thing I want hon. members to recall is that if we were earnest in advocating the lowering of the age limit, we do not want to brush it off in this house with a motion saying that we are not prepared to pass an amendment in this house to implement the sales tax. I am concerned about Nova Scotia because I know that, unless some new sources of revenue are found, there is not much chance of going through with lowering the age limit to 65. From correspondence I receive and from hundreds of people who visit me when I am back home I know it is in that large group that there is real suffering. Many women who have raised families and have no income are in that large group, and every one of them looks forward to something being done and done quickly. By the look of things now it would appear to me that it might be held off for some considerable time.
I should like to say that in my own province, in lieu of a sales tax, there are things that could be done to raise additional money. For example, there is quite a large gypsum industry in that province. The raw materials are shipped out to the United States. Millions of dollars are lost in the province in the application of royalties. Additional revenue could be raised in that province from that source. The royalty on the sale of coal that was fixed away back many years ago could be stepped up one or two cents and a lot of revenue could be received in that way. I notice that last year the total liquor sales amounted to $21,058,000.52. A five or ten per cent tax on that, or an increase in the price of it, would bring considerable revenue to that province. These methods of raising the additional money to implement the pension at 65 to 69 are things that should be done before we adopt the practice of giving the provinces the right to apply that indirect tax; because as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) pointed out, it is very definitely a change in the whole tax structure.
Anyone who went over some of the Sirois report will agree that that report pretty nearly wrote a new constitution for Canada, and particularly the allocations of the taxation fields suggested in that very comprehensive report. Therefore there are a lot of things that we could do by way of allocating revenue other than changing the constitution to give the provinces the right to apply indirect taxes.
The only reason that I rose was to point this out. Let us not forget for a minute that TVhile some of the provinces may be able to
[Mr. Gillls.)
proceed to implement to the full the old age pension proposals that we have been considering for years, yet there are many of the provinces that cannot implement these proposals without some additional ways and means of raising revenue. The best way may be a revision of the agreements between the dominion and the provinces.
No figures are available as to what it is going to cost each province, except what the premiers of Newfoundland and Saskatchewan have said. Some hon. members to whom I have talked will argue that it is not going to cost the provinces any more when they are not contributing on the original basis of 25 per cent; that that 25 per cent is revenue that they are going to have. That is quite true, but at the same time the picture is not going to be the same in every province. It certainly is not going to be the same in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, because in that age group 65 to 69 I am safe in saying you will almost double the number of people on pension. It is much easier to find, say in Newfoundland, 25 per cent of $40 for 11,000 people than it is to find 50 per cent of $40 for 22,000 people, and the picture will change from province to province. I believe it is well for the House of Commons to make up its mind that, so far as we are concerned, the right to change the British North America Act is the prerogative of the House of Commons. We have that say, in the final analysis, regardless of what the provinces may think. And it is right for us to make that known, because there is a dominion-provincial conference coming up in a day or so. This matter is going to be gone into again; and if the premiers are depending upon implementing old age pensions by that method of taxation, then it is just as well for them to know that, so far as we are concerned, we are not prepared to go along with them. We say other means must be devised to raise the additional revenue necessary to bring about full implementation of the old age pension program.

Mr. Speaker, there is one point in this connection which I think would stand some stressing, a point which has not been greatly stressed, or at least not so much as some others have.
It will be within the memory of 'hon. members that this question was debated some fifteen years ago-the very same point we have before us now. At that time they backed away from it and the great point made then, which as I understand was given, effect to at that time, is that it was really' creating a situation where it would be possible to have tariffs between provinces. I say at once to

the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that the form of the proposed resolution, at this time attempts to remove that difficulty-but I shall have a word to say about that later.
Let me read from a speech made on May 19, 1936, by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was then leader of the opposition in the Senate. He says this-something with which I am sure we would all agree-
But hon. members undoubtedly realize that there never could have been a dominion of Canada unless the power to tax by customs and excise was taken from the provinces and reposed in the dominion.
Under questioning at that time as to what the possibilities of such discrimination were the speaker, Mr. Meighen, gave an illustration from New Brunswick where, actually, an attempt had been made to give effect to that kind of discriminatory legislation. I am not sure that it ever was given effect to, but it was on the statute books. It may be that it never got past the stage of validity tests. Undoubtedly, however, it was a clear attempt to impose certain restricted taxes on certain companies. As Mr. Meighen saidi-
If goods are manufactured within the province the tax does not apply; if they are manufactured outside the province the tax does apply.
I need not labour that point further, because I am sure if members felt there was a substantial danger of that happening, there would be no disposition whatever to support a resolution of this kind. Therefore I continue for the moment to refer to that particular aspect of the matter.
In this connection I would read from a staff article appearing in the Financial Post of January 27. It raises the question and, while it does not pretend to lay down any dogmatic conclusions, it raises certain questions which were in my own mind. Because one knows that the world is full of ingenious lawyers, when I read the wording of the proposed amendment the question in my mind was: With all the facilities and with all the intricacies of company structure and company relationships, I would think that there would be some people ingenious enough, if not entirely to evade the aim of the resolution, at any rate to create such legal and other difficulties that the world would be filled with cases trying to interpret the section.
I turn now to this article in the Financial Post, because it puts very plainly the point I wish to bring before the house and which it seems to me, even if there is any substantial danger of its happening, should be sufficient to deter us from having any truck or trade with this plan. This staff article, speaking of the proposal, says:
It is also said to be open to wide possibilities of discrimination as between firms with head office in or outside the province.

On this latter criticism of "discrimination," it is claimed here that something can and will be done to prevent abuse if and when it arises, but that this matter has not been broached now because Ottawa would not wish to imply that any province would be likely to be guilty of applying the proposed amendment in discriminating fashion.
It is delightful to read of the charitable and magnanimous nature of Ottawa. But we have already got considerable evidence that it is not a matter of theory, but rather a matter of tactics. The provinces would be very glad to avail themselves of the right to discriminate, if the way was open for them to do so. I continue to read:
In the draft legislation forwarded to the provinces, there is a safeguard against any tax which would hinder interprovincial trade, but none specifically aimed at the more subtle discrimination that might arise if the provincial authority were to pass regulations to favour firms with head office within its own boundaries.
That of course was done in the case of the New Brunswick statute to which I referred a short time ago. And, without labouring the matter further, I think it would be very unrealistic to dismiss as quite impossible devices of that kind. I do not think we should undertake to sit in judgment on the provinces concerned, either. Once they get this right they will be wanting to use it for the benefit of their own citizens. That is their duty; that is what they are elected for. And if we are to abandon this primary safeguard which the fathers of confederation thought was essential, and which fifteen years ago was thought so essential that legislation, as I understand it, was then abandoned, it seems to me we ought to stop, look and listen.
There is one other point I wish to bring out from this same issue of the Financial Post. This is a very interesting statement made by Mr. J. R. Petrie, director of research of the Canadian Tax Foundation, and a recognized tax expert. I read this brief paragraph from what he says. After making various other comments, he added:
The year 1951 is likely to be a turning point in our peacetime fiscal history. Important policy decisions are in the making. As important as any is the decision on sales tax policy. There is still time to reappraise our over-all requirements and to formulate a policy which will really reach the root of the sales tax problem.
If the current proposals, which are not yet public, simply involve a concession to the provinces to levy indirect sales tax, even though some limitation be placed on me concession, uiey represent a retreat from the problem rather than a solution to it. Constructive policy is needed urgently. Now is the time to produce it.
The only observation I wish to add is that, notwithstanding what the Prime Minister said as to the position of the House of Commons-the house seems like a conduit

pipe for forwarding the views of the provinces, though perhaps that is an exaggeration -it does seem to me that if we wait until the provinces, let us say, have agreed to recommend a certain course, then I would have thought it would be extremely difficult for this House of Commons to snub them by saying, "You all wanted it, but now you cannot have it".
I understood the Prime Minister this afternoon to go to the length of saying that if, in fact, the ten provinces came along and asked for it, the matter was pretty well decided, so far as we are concerned. If I understood him correctly he said that if that happened he would then submit the matter to his colleagues and-again, if my recollection is right-the matter would be put before the house. The Prime Minister seemed to indicate that we were merely going to leave it to the provinces. I felt that he felt that it would be rather improper for us to have views on this, but I suggest that if we do not have views now it may be practically too late for us to have them later on.

for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) mentioned the agreements between Ottawa and the provinces in connection with the assumption of responsibility for the payment of pensions to needy persons between the ages of 65 and 69 years.

If all the provinces are in unison, if they all agree, what can we do? If that is the general desire of the people, can we place obstacles in their way?
